title: PostgreSQL Delete Duplicate Rows but Keep One: 4 Methods
description: Delete duplicate rows in PostgreSQL but keep one: DELETE USING, row_number(), ctid for tables without an id, the NULL trap and a unique constraint.
focusKeyword: postgresql delete duplicate rows but keep one

sources.title: PostgreSQL 18 docs: Comparison Functions and Operators (IS NOT DISTINCT FROM)
PostgreSQL 18 docs: Constraints (unique, NULLS NOT DISTINCT)

reviewNotes: Regular Sunday article (not a series part). Topic from Google autocomplete: 'postgresql delete duplicate rows but keep one' (top suggestion), plus '... without id', '... multiple columns', '... keep one'. No live article or earlier PostgreSQL draft covers it (an Oracle draft on the same question exists, 2026-10-24). Current top results (wiki, neon tutorial, GeeksforGeeks) show DELETE USING and row_number() but miss the NULL trap with =, ctid for keyless tables, case-insensitive duplicates and NULLS NOT DISTINCT. TEST ENVIRONMENT: Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS with PostgreSQL 18.7 (18.7-1.pgdg24.04+5, official PGDG binaries). As in earlier runs, apt could not install postgresql-18 (dependency liburing2 not installable in the sandbox), so I extracted the PGDG .debs and ran initdb/pg_ctl/psql from them with a stub liburing (io_method=worker, the default). All outputs are real psql output; each method was run on freshly reloaded sample data, as the captions say. Docs followed: PostgreSQL 18 documentation at /docs/18/ (postgresql.org/docs/current now shows version 19). EDITOR CHECKS: (1) The case-insensitive section runs after the unique-constraint section on the same data, which is why the ids are {1,9} (id 8 consumed by the rejected insert); the article explains this. (2) The statement that GROUP BY/PARTITION BY/DISTINCT group NULLs together is shown by the test output, not quoted from the docs. (3) Batching advice is general guidance with no example.

data.text: To delete duplicate rows in PostgreSQL but keep one, delete every row that has a twin with a smaller id: DELETE FROM t a USING t b WHERE a.col = b.col AND a.id > b.id. If you need to choose which copy survives (the newest, the most complete), number the copies with row_number() and delete everything numbered above 1. If the table has no id column at all, use the hidden system column ctid instead.

This tutorial shows all three methods on small sample tables, with the real output from PostgreSQL 18. It also covers the two traps that catch most people, NULL values and upper/lower case, and how to stop duplicates from coming back with a unique constraint.
What counts as a duplicate, and which row to keep

Before you write any DELETE, answer two questions. First, which columns define a duplicate? Two customer rows may be "the same customer" when the email matches, even if the city differs. Second, which copy should survive? The oldest row, the newest row, or any one of them?

PostgreSQL has no special "remove duplicates" command. You write an ordinary DELETE whose WHERE clause picks every row except the one you want to keep. The methods below differ only in how they pick that survivor.

content: The table has a unique id and any copy is fine
You must choose the survivor by a rule, such as newest date
Row numbered 1 by your ORDER BY
The table has no primary key (raw imports, staging tables)
Most of a large table is duplicated
One copy of each distinct row

data.text: Sample setup

Create a scratch database and a customers table where the same email was registered more than once. The primary key is an identity column, so every row has its own customer_id even when the rest of the row is a copy.

data.code:
CREATE TABLE customers (
    customer_id  bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    email        text NOT NULL,
    full_name    text NOT NULL,
    city         text,
    signup_date  date NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO customers (email, full_name, city, signup_date) VALUES
  ('asha@example.com',  'Asha Rao',     'Pune',      '2026-01-05'),
  ('ravi@example.com',  'Ravi Kumar',   'Chennai',   '2026-01-06'),
  ('asha@example.com',  'Asha Rao',     'Pune',      '2026-02-10'),
  ('meera@example.com', 'Meera Iyer',   'Bengaluru', '2026-02-11'),
  ('ravi@example.com',  'Ravi Kumar',   'Hyderabad', '2026-03-01'),
  ('asha@example.com',  'Asha R.',      'Mumbai',    '2026-03-20'),
  ('john@example.com',  'John Mathew',  'Kochi',     '2026-03-22');
data.caption: Sample table with duplicate emails

data.code:
CREATE TABLE
INSERT 0 7
data.caption: Output

data.text: Step 1: find the duplicates first

Always look before you delete. GROUP BY the columns that define a duplicate and keep only the groups with more than one row. array_agg lists the ids in each group so you can see exactly what is at stake.

data.code:
SELECT email, count(*) AS copies, min(customer_id) AS keep_id,
       array_agg(customer_id ORDER BY customer_id) AS all_ids
  FROM customers
 GROUP BY email
HAVING count(*) > 1
 ORDER BY email;
data.caption: List duplicate emails and their ids
Output

data.text: Two emails are duplicated: asha has three rows and ravi has two. If we keep the lowest id in each group, rows 3, 5 and 6 must go, which is 3 rows. Write that number down; the DELETE should report the same count.
Method 1: DELETE USING a self-join (keep the lowest id)

DELETE ... USING lets the WHERE clause refer to another table. Here the "other table" is the same customers table under a second alias. The documentation for DELETE says that when you repeat the target table in USING for a self-join, it must have an alias, which is why we write customers a and customers b.
The condition reads: delete row a if there is another row b with the same email and a smaller id. The row with the smallest id never has a smaller twin, so it survives.

data.caption: Delete duplicates inside a transaction

data.code:
BEGIN
 customer_id |      email       
-------------+------------------
           3 | asha@example.com
           5 | ravi@example.com
           6 | asha@example.com
(3 rows)

DELETE 3
data.caption: Output

data.text: RETURNING prints every deleted row, and the command tag DELETE 3 matches the count we expected from Step 1. Because we started with BEGIN, nothing is final yet. Check the table, then decide.

data.code: SELECT customer_id, email, city FROM customers ORDER BY customer_id;
data.caption: Check what is left

data.code:
customer_id |       email       |   city    
-------------+-------------------+-----------
           1 | asha@example.com  | Pune
           2 | ravi@example.com  | Chennai
           4 | meera@example.com | Bengaluru
           7 | john@example.com  | Kochi
(4 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: One row per email, and the oldest ids survived. Run COMMIT; to keep the change, or ROLLBACK; if anything looks wrong. To keep the highest id instead, flip the comparison to a.customer_id < b.customer_id.
Wrap every duplicate cleanup in BEGIN ... COMMIT and compare the DELETE count with your Step 1 query. A ROLLBACK costs nothing; restoring a backup costs a lot.
Method 2: row_number() to choose which copy survives

The lowest id is not always the right survivor. In our data, Ravi's newer row says Hyderabad and Asha's newest row says Mumbai, which may be their current cities. To keep the newest signup for each email, you need a rule, and that is what a window function gives you.

row_number() "returns the number of the current row within its partition, counting from 1" (PostgreSQL documentation). PARTITION BY email starts a new count for each email, and the ORDER BY inside OVER decides which row gets number 1.
Step 1: preview the numbering

data.code:
SELECT customer_id, email, signup_date,
       row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY email
                          ORDER BY signup_date DESC, customer_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM customers
 ORDER BY email, rn;
data.caption: Number the copies, newest first (run on fresh sample data)

data.code:
customer_id |       email       | signup_date | rn 
-------------+-------------------+-------------+----
           6 | asha@example.com  | 2026-03-20  |  1
           3 | asha@example.com  | 2026-02-10  |  2
           1 | asha@example.com  | 2026-01-05  |  3
           7 | john@example.com  | 2026-03-22  |  1
           4 | meera@example.com | 2026-02-11  |  1
           5 | ravi@example.com  | 2026-03-01  |  1
           2 | ravi@example.com  | 2026-01-06  |  2
(7 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: The newest row of each email gets rn = 1. Every row with rn greater than 1 is a copy to delete. customer_id DESC is a tie-breaker: if two copies share the same signup_date, the numbering is still predictable instead of random.
Step 2: delete the rows numbered above 1
You cannot put a window function straight into WHERE. PostgreSQL rejects it:

data.code: SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY customer_id) > 1;
data.caption: This fails

data.code:
ERROR:  window functions are not allowed in WHERE
LINE 1: SELECT customer_id FROM customers WHERE row_number() OVER (P...
                                                ^
data.caption: Output

data.text: The documentation explains why: window functions run after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING have been processed. The fix is to compute the number in a subquery and filter it outside:

data.code:
BEGIN;

DELETE FROM customers
 WHERE customer_id IN (
       SELECT customer_id
         FROM (SELECT customer_id,
                      row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY email
                                         ORDER BY signup_date DESC, customer_id DESC) AS rn
                 FROM customers) ranked
        WHERE rn > 1)
RETURNING customer_id, email, city, signup_date;
data.caption: Keep the newest row per email

data.code:
BEGIN
 customer_id |      email       |  city   | signup_date 
-------------+------------------+---------+-------------
           1 | asha@example.com | Pune    | 2026-01-05
           2 | ravi@example.com | Chennai | 2026-01-06
           3 | asha@example.com | Pune    | 2026-02-10
(3 rows)

DELETE 3
data.caption: Output

data.code: SELECT customer_id, email, city, signup_date FROM customers ORDER BY email;
data.caption: Verify, then COMMIT

data.code:
customer_id |       email       |   city    | signup_date 
-------------+-------------------+-----------+-------------
           6 | asha@example.com  | Mumbai    | 2026-03-20
           7 | john@example.com  | Kochi     | 2026-03-22
           4 | meera@example.com | Bengaluru | 2026-02-11
           5 | ravi@example.com  | Hyderabad | 2026-03-01
(4 rows)
data.caption: Output

data.text: This time the newest rows survived (ids 6 and 5). To define duplicates by more than one column, list them all in PARTITION BY, for example PARTITION BY email, full_name. If you only want to read one row per group without deleting anything, DISTINCT ON is shorter; see PostgreSQL DISTINCT ON: one row per group.
Method 3: no primary key? Use ctid

Raw imports and staging tables often have no id at all, and the copies are identical in every column. There is no column that tells them apart, so Methods 1 and 2 have nothing to compare. PostgreSQL still has one: every table has a hidden system column called ctid.
ctid is the physical location of a row version inside the table: a page number and a position on that page, such as (0,2). You do not see it with SELECT *, but you can ask for it by name.

data.code:
CREATE TABLE payment_import (
    payment_ref  text,
    order_no     integer,
    amount       numeric(10,2),
    paid_via     text
);

INSERT INTO payment_import VALUES
  ('PAY-101', 5001, 1499.00, 'UPI'),
  ('PAY-101', 5001, 1499.00, 'UPI'),
  ('PAY-102', 5002,  899.50, 'Card'),
  ('PAY-103', 5003,  250.00, NULL),
  ('PAY-103', 5003,  250.00, NULL),
  ('PAY-103', 5003,  250.00, NULL),
  ('PAY-104', 5004, 3200.00, 'NetBanking');
data.caption: A payment import table with no primary key

data.code: SELECT ctid, * FROM payment_import;
data.caption: Show the hidden ctid column

data.text: PAY-101 appears twice and PAY-103 three times, so 3 rows should be deleted. PAY-103 has no paid_via value: it is NULL. That detail matters.
The NULL trap
Here is the self-join from Method 1 with ctid in place of the id:

data.caption: Looks right, but misses rows

data.code:
BEGIN
DELETE 1
ROLLBACK
data.caption: Output

data.text: Only 1 row was deleted, not 3. The PAY-103 copies survived because NULL = NULL is not true; it is NULL, meaning "unknown", and WHERE only keeps rows where the condition is true. The documentation's fix is IS NOT DISTINCT FROM, which works like = but treats two NULLs as equal.

data.code:
BEGIN;

DELETE FROM payment_import a
 USING payment_import b
 WHERE a.payment_ref IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.payment_ref
   AND a.order_no    IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.order_no
   AND a.amount      IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.amount
   AND a.paid_via    IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.paid_via
   AND a.ctid > b.ctid
RETURNING a.ctid, a.payment_ref;
data.caption: NULL-safe comparison

data.code:
BEGIN
 ctid  | payment_ref 
-------+-------------
 (0,2) | PAY-101
 (0,5) | PAY-103
 (0,6) | PAY-103
(3 rows)

DELETE 3
data.caption: Output

data.text: Now all 3 copies are found. Notice that the GROUP BY check from Step 1 would have counted PAY-103 correctly, because GROUP BY and PARTITION BY put NULLs in the same group. That makes the row_number() version NULL-safe without any extra work:

data.code:
DELETE FROM payment_import
 WHERE ctid IN (
       SELECT ctid
         FROM (SELECT ctid,
                      row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY payment_ref, order_no, amount, paid_via
                                         ORDER BY ctid) AS rn
                 FROM payment_import) ranked
        WHERE rn > 1);
data.caption: row_number() with ctid (NULLs grouped together)

data.code: DELETE 3
data.caption: Output

data.code: SELECT ctid, * FROM payment_import;
data.caption: Verify

data.text: The PostgreSQL documentation warns that a row's ctid changes when the row is updated or moved by VACUUM FULL, so ctid should not be used as a row identifier. Using it inside one DELETE statement is fine, because it is read and used in the same statement. Never save ctid values and use them later, and add a real primary key to the table once it is clean.
Method 4: most rows are duplicates? Rebuild the table

When a large share of a big table is duplicated, deleting row by row leaves many dead rows behind and can take a long time. Copying the distinct rows out, emptying the table and loading them back is often simpler. Using TRUNCATE on the original table (instead of dropping it) keeps its grants, indexes, views and triggers in place.

data.caption: Rebuild with only distinct rows (run on fresh sample data)

data.code:
BEGIN
SELECT 4
TRUNCATE TABLE
INSERT 0 4
COMMIT
data.caption: Output

data.text: SELECT 4 means four distinct rows were saved, and INSERT 0 4 means all four went back. SELECT DISTINCT also treats NULLs as equal, so the three PAY-103 copies became one.

TRUNCATE takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, which blocks all other reads and writes on the table until COMMIT; the documentation says to use DELETE instead when concurrent access is needed. TRUNCATE also refuses to run on a table that other tables reference with foreign keys, unless you add CASCADE, which empties those tables too. Do not use CASCADE here. Take a backup first and run this in a maintenance window on production systems.
Stop duplicates from coming back

Cleaning up is half the job. If the application can still insert the same email twice, you will be back here next month. A unique constraint makes PostgreSQL reject the duplicate at insert time. Adding one creates a unique B-tree index on the columns.
If you try to add it before cleaning up, it fails and tells you one of the offending values:

data.code: ALTER TABLE customers ADD CONSTRAINT customers_email_key UNIQUE (email);
data.caption: Before cleanup (fresh sample data)

data.code:
ERROR:  could not create unique index "customers_email_key"
DETAIL:  Key (email)=(ravi@example.com) is duplicated.
data.caption: Output

data.text: After running Method 1 and committing, the same statement succeeds, and a repeated email is rejected:

data.caption: After cleanup

data.code:
ALTER TABLE
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "customers_email_key"
DETAIL:  Key (email)=(asha@example.com) already exists.
data.caption: Output

data.text: If the application should update the existing row instead of failing, use INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, explained in PostgreSQL upsert with ON CONFLICT.
Unique constraints and NULLs

By default, a unique constraint treats NULLs as different from each other, so the duplicate PAY-103 rows (paid_via is NULL) would still be allowed. Since PostgreSQL 15 you can add NULLS NOT DISTINCT so that NULLs count as equal:

data.caption: Treat NULLs as equal (PostgreSQL 15 and later)

data.code:
ALTER TABLE
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "payment_import_uq"
DETAIL:  Key (payment_ref, order_no, amount, paid_via)=(PAY-103, 5003, 250.00, null) already exists.
data.caption: Output

data.text: Without NULLS NOT DISTINCT, the same INSERT succeeded in our test and created a new duplicate.
Common mistakes
Deleting every copy, including the one to keep

DELETE FROM customers WHERE email IN (SELECT email FROM customers GROUP BY email HAVING count(*) > 1) removes all rows for those emails, not just the extras. The query must leave one row per group untouched, which is what a.customer_id > b.customer_id or rn > 1 does.
Using <> instead of > in the self-join
With a.customer_id <> b.customer_id, every row in a group has a different twin, so every copy matches and all of them are deleted. Always use > or <, never <>.
Missing duplicates that differ only in case
To text comparison, Asha@Example.com and asha@example.com are different values, so the unique constraint above lets both in:

data.code:
INSERT INTO customers (email, full_name, city, signup_date)
VALUES ('Asha@Example.com', 'Asha Rao', 'Pune', '2026-04-01');
data.caption: Accepted, although it is the same person

data.code: INSERT 0 1
data.caption: Output

data.text: Group by an expression to find such duplicates:

data.code:
SELECT lower(email) AS email_key, array_agg(customer_id ORDER BY customer_id) AS ids
  FROM customers
 GROUP BY lower(email)
HAVING count(*) > 1;
data.caption: Find case-insensitive duplicates

data.code:
email_key     |  ids  
------------------+-------
 asha@example.com | {1,9}
(1 row)
data.caption: Output

data.text: Id 8 is missing because the rejected INSERT earlier still used up an identity value; failed inserts leave gaps. Delete with the same expression, then protect the table with a unique index on the expression:

data.caption: Clean up and prevent case-insensitive duplicates

data.code:
DELETE 1
CREATE INDEX
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "customers_email_lower_key"
DETAIL:  Key (lower(email))=(asha@example.com) already exists.
data.caption: Output

data.text: Forgetting the child tables

If orders reference customer_id 3 and you delete customer 3, the foreign key either blocks the DELETE or, with ON DELETE CASCADE, silently deletes those orders. Before removing duplicate parents, point the child rows at the surviving id with an UPDATE, in the same transaction.
Performance tips

items.content: Index the columns that define a duplicate (here email) before running the self-join on a large table. Without an index, PostgreSQL may have to compare the table with itself the hard way.
The row_number() method reads the table once and sorts it, which usually behaves well when there are many duplicates.

DELETE does not shrink the table. Deleted rows become dead row versions that VACUUM cleans up later; see MVCC and row visibility. After a large cleanup, run VACUUM (ANALYZE) customers; and check for bloat as shown in Part 13: table and index bloat.
For millions of rows on a busy system, delete in batches (for example, one range of ids per transaction) so each transaction holds row locks for a short time and VACUUM can keep up.
DELETE lets other sessions keep reading and writing the table; TRUNCATE (Method 4) blocks them all. Pick the method that fits the time window you have.

data.text: Frequently asked questions
How do I delete duplicate rows in PostgreSQL without an id?

Use the ctid system column as a temporary tie-breaker: DELETE FROM t a USING t b WHERE a.col IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.col AND a.ctid > b.ctid, listing every column. Use it only within that one statement, and add a primary key afterwards.
How do I delete duplicates based on multiple columns?
List all the columns in the join condition (a.email = b.email AND a.full_name = b.full_name) or in PARTITION BY email, full_name. Columns you leave out are allowed to differ between the copies.
How do I keep the latest duplicate row instead of the first?

Use row_number() with ORDER BY signup_date DESC, customer_id DESC in the OVER clause and delete rows where rn > 1, as in Method 2. With the self-join, a.customer_id < b.customer_id keeps the highest id.
Can I undo a DELETE of duplicates?
Only before COMMIT. Inside BEGIN, a ROLLBACK restores everything. After COMMIT, the rows can only come back from a backup, which is why every example here runs in a transaction and is checked first.
Summary

items.content: Decide which columns define a duplicate and which copy should survive.
Find the duplicates first with GROUP BY ... HAVING count(*) > 1 and note how many rows should go.
Use DELETE ... USING with a.id > b.id to keep the lowest id.
Use row_number() in a subquery when the survivor depends on a rule, such as the newest date.
Use ctid for tables without a key, only inside a single statement.
Compare nullable columns with IS NOT DISTINCT FROM, never with =.
Run the DELETE inside BEGIN, check the count and the remaining rows, then COMMIT.
Add a UNIQUE constraint (NULLS NOT DISTINCT, or a unique index on lower(email), if needed) so duplicates cannot return.
Run VACUUM (ANALYZE) after a large cleanup.

linkedin.post:
Your DELETE removed 1 duplicate row, but there were 3. The reason is a NULL.

Cleaning duplicates in PostgreSQL while keeping one copy is a common task. Here is what works:

→ Keep the lowest id with a self-join: DELETE ... USING the same table under a second alias, and delete a row when a twin with the same email and a smaller customer_id exists. Use > there, never <>

→ Need the newest copy instead? Number the copies with row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY signup_date DESC) in a subquery and delete rn > 1

→ No primary key at all? The hidden ctid column tells identical rows apart. Use it inside one statement only, it changes after UPDATE and VACUUM FULL

→ NULL = NULL is not true, so copies with NULL columns survive a plain = join. Compare with IS NOT DISTINCT FROM

→ Then add a UNIQUE constraint (NULLS NOT DISTINCT since PostgreSQL 15) so duplicates cannot come back

Run it all inside BEGIN and check the DELETE count before COMMIT.

Which one do you reach for first: the self-join or row_number()?

slides.title: Delete Duplicates, Keep One Row
slides.body: Four PostgreSQL methods, tested on PostgreSQL 18

slides.title: Step 1: find them first
points: GROUP BY the columns that define a duplicate
Note how many rows should be deleted
slides.code:
SELECT email, count(*)
  FROM customers
 GROUP BY email
HAVING count(*) > 1;

slides.title: Keep the lowest id
slides.body: Join the table to itself. Delete a row when a twin with a smaller id exists. Use > not <>, or every copy is deleted.
slides.code:
DELETE FROM customers a
 USING customers b
 WHERE a.email = b.email
   AND a.customer_id > b.customer_id;

slides.title: Keep the newest copy
points: Number copies per email with row_number()
ORDER BY signup_date DESC gives the newest rn = 1
Filter rn > 1 in an outer query, not in WHERE
slides.code:
SELECT customer_id,
  row_number() OVER (
    PARTITION BY email
    ORDER BY signup_date DESC) AS rn
FROM customers;

slides.title: No id? Use ctid, carefully
points: ctid is the hidden physical row location
It changes after UPDATE or VACUUM FULL
Use it inside one statement, then add a key

slides.title: The NULL trap
slides.body: NULL = NULL is not true, so rows with NULL columns escape a plain = join. Use IS NOT DISTINCT FROM, then add UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (PostgreSQL 15+) to block new copies.
